A Baroque church on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini with Giovanni de'Rossi for the novices of the Jesuits. Cardinal Camillo Pamphili paid for it, with the approval of Pope Alexander VII. Bernini took the commission in 1658, the church was built by 1661, and the decoration was finished in 1670. It was the third Jesuit church in Rome, after the Gesù and Sant'Ignazio. Bernini counted it among his most perfect works; his son recalled that in old age he would sit inside it for hours.

The church is an oval entered on its short side, so the door looks straight at the high altar across the width of the room. Outside, it stands back from the street behind low curved walls, with a half-round porch on two columns under the Pamphili arms. Inside, the side chapels are dark and the altar niche is lit from a hidden source. Over the altar hangs a painting of the martyrdom of Saint Andrew by Guillaume Courtois, and above it a white stucco figure of the saint by Antonio Raggi rises on a cloud through the broken pediment toward the gilded dome and the dove of the Holy Spirit in the lantern. Bernini joined painting, sculpture and architecture to tell one story, as he did in the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.

A chapel holds the shrine of the Jesuit novice Saint Stanislaus Kostka, and his rooms in the house next door have been rebuilt, with a marble figure of the dying saint by Pierre Legros. Charles Emmanuel IV, King of Sardinia, who gave up his throne to become a Jesuit, is buried here. The church stands on the same street as San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, the first church of Bernini's rival Francesco Borromini.
